text: When a software vendor ships a Kubernetes application to a customer, they often give up the one thing they need to debug it: access. The customer runs it in their own disconnected cluster. So when something breaks, the vendor's engineers can't kubectl in, can't tail a log, can't poke at a failing pod. All they get is a support bundle — a tarball the Troubleshoot tool collects from the cluster, full of logs, events, resource manifests, and node state. A frozen snapshot of a sick system. And making sense of it is a manual craft: it takes an engineer who knows Kubernetes failure modes by heart, and hours of correlating signals across dozens of files by hand. This is Triage. It automates that first pass.

I'll run it against a sample bundle from a fictional store called acme-shop. When I start, Triage extracts the archive and walks the whole tree. Instead of hard-coding paths, it parses every resource and buckets it by its Kubernetes kind — pods, deployments, events, nodes, volume claims — so it stays robust when bundle layouts differ between versions. Then it runs a catalog of deterministic detectors over that model, and hands the findings to a language model to reason about. Watch — it finishes in about a second.

Here's the report. The verdict is critical — but it doesn't just say 'errors found,' it names the actual problem in plain language. Underneath are the cluster's vital signs: Kubernetes one twenty-seven, three nodes, three namespaces, and only eight of twenty-one pods actually running. Thirteen are failing. So this isn't a glitch — a real chunk of the application is down, and the job is to understand why.

This is the heart of it. The summary doesn't just list problems — it explains them. And it has worked out that these failures aren't eight separate incidents. They're one root cause with a cascade. A Postgres database can't start, because its storage claim asks for a storage class called fast-ssd that doesn't exist in this cluster — only one named standard does. With no database, the checkout and payments services can't connect, so they flood their logs with 'connection refused.' Here's the part that matters: Triage labels those connection errors as symptoms, not bugs. It separates the one thing you need to fix from the noise it produces. And it ranks the likely root causes, each with a confidence level and the exact findings it's based on. Nothing is invented.

If the summary is the 'what,' the Findings tab is the 'prove it.' Every finding is ranked by severity and tagged by category. Let me open the storage one. It shows the volume claim stuck Pending, the missing storage class confirmed against the classes that actually exist, and the scheduling event from Kubernetes itself — each quoted with the exact file path it came from. That's what makes it trustworthy: when you can't log in, the tool has to show its work, and it does. Now a separate problem — the payments service is being killed for exceeding its memory limit, over and over, in a crash loop. The evidence is the exit code, one thirty-seven, and a Java out-of-memory error from the pod's own log. And I can filter, by severity or category, to focus on the structural problems.

Diagnosis is only half the job. The Remediation tab turns the findings into an ordered plan. It says fix the storage first — not arbitrarily, but because it's the highest-impact change: repairing the database clears the whole cascade of connection errors for free. Then raise the payments memory limit and bound the heap. Then fix the image and the missing config key. Each step has a rationale and concrete kubectl commands. This is something you could hand straight to whoever's on call.

Two more views. The Cluster tab is the inventory: here's node-2, gone NotReady and under memory and disk pressure, which shrinks the capacity the scheduler can use — next to every workload and its ready-versus-desired count. And the Evidence tab gathers every raw excerpt the report was built from into one place, so a skeptical engineer can audit the reasoning end to end.

To prove it isn't just pattern-matching doom onto everything, here's the same tool on a healthy bundle. Green verdict, no issues. And worth knowing: Triage runs even without an AI key — the detectors still produce the full evidence-backed report, and only the narrative falls back to a deterministic summary. Every analysis is saved to History, so you can reopen any past report.

So that's Triage. The design bet is what makes it trustworthy: deterministic detectors do the grounded, precise work and cite their evidence, and the language model does what it's good at — correlation and explanation — but only ever over facts the detectors already established. That's the guardrail against hallucination, which is exactly what you can't do without when you're debugging a system you'll never get to touch. From here, the next steps are a rule language to codify fixes once, and bundle-to-bundle diffing to pinpoint what changed. Thanks for watching.
